# Structuring AI-Assisted Design Work {#sec-architecture-20-ontology}

::: {.epigraph}
> *"All models are wrong, but some are useful."*
>
> — George E. P. Box, *Robustness in the Strategy of Scientific Model Building* (1979) [@Box1979Robustness]
:::

::: {.column-margin}
**Author's Note:** George E. P. Box, a British statistician, coined this
aphorism about statistical models. Every model simplifies, and the working
question is whether the simplification still serves the decision at hand. A
task description, benchmark, simulator, power model, or test suite always leaves
something out. Each can still be useful when its scope and failure modes are
clear and when the decision does not reach beyond the evidence it provides.
:::

::: {.callout-crux}
How should an architect turn diagnosed but still informal work into a bounded
study that can support a decision or stop honestly?
:::

@sec-design-loop-no-longer-scales ended with a specific diagnosis. During a
fifteen-working-day window, mobile XR finalist packages arrived for thermal and
IR-drop review faster than qualified reviewers could clear them. The
observations supported overloaded review for that work item and window, with
input churn adding rework. They did not show that search or simulation limited
other work. They also left one requirement intact. Any intervention still had
to preserve the thermal and IR-drop verdicts.

That diagnosis is useful, but it is not yet a study. It does not state which
architecture decision a finalist package should support, what it should be
compared with, which changes are permitted, which measurements must be present,
how much work the project will spend, or what causes the work to stop. Choosing
a method before declaring those items would automate an underspecified task.

This chapter supplies the missing structure. It first turns one piece of
diagnosed architecture work into a bounded study. It then presents six stages
as a useful default for carrying that study forward. The stages are not a
universal schedule and they do not organize the rest of the book. A boundary is
useful only when adjacent work answers a different question, produces a
different output, or requires a different repair. The chapter closes with the
skeleton of one cumulative study record, leaving the representation, method,
environment, executed results, and final decision open for the chapters that
own them.

::: {.callout-learning-objectives}
After reading this chapter, you can:

- Turn a diagnosed work item and preserved check into a study contract that
  names the question, comparator, scope, permitted changes, constraints,
  conditions, planned measurements and checks, budget, stopping conditions,
  intended decision, and exclusions.
- Decide whether two kinds of work need separate stages by comparing their
  questions, outputs, inadequacy conditions, and repair paths.
- Distinguish an infrastructure failure, a rejected candidate, an unresolved
  comparison, a completed decision, and a budget stop.
- Trace one bounded Lighthouse study through Formulate, Explore, Implement,
  Evaluate, Explain, and Review and Decide without treating that sequence as a
  rigid process.
- Start a cumulative study record whose missing entries remain visible to the
  next architect.

:::

## From a Diagnosed Constraint to a Bounded Study {#sec-arch2-ontology}

An architecture project needs a common unit of work between a broad product
goal and the tools used to investigate it. @fig-structured-layer-above-rtl
places a structured study in that position. The study preserves the question,
comparison, execution plan, and review scope that let architects interpret
otherwise disconnected artifacts and tool results.

![**A structured architecture study connects intent to implementation evidence.** The study contains the scope, architectural claim, execution and analysis process, and records needed for review. Iterative work may use a design loop.](images/F4d-structured-layer-above-rtl){#fig-structured-layer-above-rtl width="85%" fig-alt="Three-layer diagram showing architecture intent and judgment flowing into a structured architecture study, with tool results flowing back for review."}

> **Bounded architecture study.** A bounded architecture study turns a broad
> goal into a specific piece of architecture work. It states the question,
> comparator, scope, permitted changes, constraints, conditions, planned
> measurements and checks, budget, stopping conditions, intended decision, and
> exclusions.

The diagnosis in @sec-design-loop-no-longer-scales concerned finalist packages
waiting for review. To make the lifecycle concrete, this chapter uses the cache
comparison inside one such package. It does not claim that cache search caused
the queue or that this comparison will reduce waiting time. Testing a
standardized package as an intervention would require a separate process study
with queue, preparation-time, rework, and unchanged-verdict measurements. Here,
the diagnosed review work supplies the delivery context and the checks that
must remain independent.

The product intent remains the Lighthouse goal of a low-power 64-bit RISC-V
mobile XR subsystem. The bounded architecture decision is much smaller. It asks
which, if either, of two larger L2 capacities should advance from analysis into
RTL evaluation.

@tbl-bounded-study-contract shows the contract before a search or method is
chosen. Its numbers are illustrative, as are the later tool returns. What
matters is that the declarations make the work and its limits inspectable.

| **Declaration** | **Mobile XR cache study** |
| --- | --- |
| Question | Which, if either, of the 3\ MB and 4\ MB L2 candidates should advance to RTL evaluation for the declared XR workload? |
| Comparator | The current 2\ MB L2 baseline. Both larger candidates are compared against the same rerun baseline. |
| Scope | One cache-capacity decision inside the compute subsystem. Cache policy, NoC topology, compiler, runtime, and the rest of the memory system remain fixed. |
| Permitted changes | L2 capacity may take the values 2\ MB, 3\ MB, or 4\ MB. No other architectural parameter may change in this study. |
| Constraints | Modeled subsystem dynamic plus leakage power must not exceed 3\ W. The cache macro must not exceed 1.5\ mm^2^, and its modeled access time must not exceed the 2.5\ ns allocation used by the 2\ GHz microarchitecture. Required thermal and IR-drop review remains independent. |
| Conditions | Workload snapshot `XR-TRACE-A`, including stable frame identifiers and boundaries; RISC-V software image `SW-BASE-A`; and recorded versions of the cycle-level simulator, cache model, power model `PM-A`, SRAM model `SRAM-A`, and process, voltage, and temperature assumptions `PVT-A`. |
| Planned measurements and checks | Measure 99th-percentile frame time, capacity misses, dynamic and leakage power, macro area, and access time. Estimate the frame-time reduction and its 95% interval with a paired block bootstrap over matched frame sequences. A capacity advances only if its physical checks pass and that interval relative to 2\ MB lies above zero. |
| Budget | Four cycle-level executions in total, including reruns after infrastructure failures, plus one SRAM timing, area, and power evaluation per declared capacity. No RTL synthesis or physical signoff is included. |
| Stopping conditions | Stop when the intended decision is resolved, all permitted capacities are exhausted, the run budget is spent, or a required input or measurement remains unavailable. |
| Intended decision | Recommend at most one cache capacity for a later RTL study. This contract does not authorize implementation, signoff, tapeout, or a product commitment. |
| Exclusions | Cache policy, prefetching, coherence, NoC changes, compiler changes, software scheduling, full floorplanning, thermal signoff, IR-drop signoff, security, reliability, and product-level cost. |

: **A study contract declares the work before a method is chosen.** The
contract connects one technical comparison to a bounded architecture decision,
while preserving the independent checks carried from the diagnosed review
work. {#tbl-bounded-study-contract tbl-colwidths="[24,76]"}

The contract is narrower than the Lighthouse prompt by design. It does not
claim that cache capacity is the most important subsystem choice or that
standardizing the package will eliminate the observed review queue. It states
what this piece of work can decide and preserves the physical reviews that the
review package must not replace.

An architectural claim gives the study a falsifiable expectation.

> **Architectural claim.** An architectural claim states the proposed
> mechanism, expected outcome, scenario, comparator, alternatives, constraints,
> and evidence that would count against it.

For this study, the primary claim is that at least one larger L2 reduces
99th-percentile XR frame time relative to the 2\ MB baseline because it removes
capacity misses while remaining inside the declared power, area, and timing
constraints. The 3\ MB and 4\ MB candidates face the same checks. The claim does
not assume that fewer capacity misses necessarily reduce frame time. It makes
that connection something the planned measurements must establish.

The claim also invites a check that costs nothing to run. If the frames or
intervals that set the tail spend 18 percent of their latency stalled on L2
capacity misses, eliminating every one of those stalls can recover at most that
fraction for those observations. This Amdahl-style ceiling
[@HillMarty2008Amdahl] does not by itself bound a percentile whose tail-setting
frames may change after the intervention. It is a first check against a claim
whose requested improvement exceeds what the named mechanism can supply.

Constraints require conditions and units before they are checkable. A 3\ W
limit and a 2\ GHz target do not identify the power components, workload state,
process corner, voltage, temperature, or guardband under which the numbers must
hold. The controlling timing corner depends on the process, library, voltage,
and path, so the study records the conditions supplied by the relevant models
instead of treating one named corner as universal. Coupled effects such as cache
banking, interconnect distance, floorplan blockage, power delivery, and
temperature remain in the contract whenever they could reverse the comparison.

::: {.callout-war-story title="Mars Climate Orbiter and the units nobody checked"}
**The claim.** The Mars Climate Orbiter navigation team consumed an impulse
value whose interface specification required newton-seconds
[@MCOMishapBoard1999].

**The gap.** Ground software supplied pound-force seconds. Each component ran,
but nothing checked the value where it crossed the interface. The 4.45
conversion error accumulated until the reconstructed closest approach was 57
km, below the planned 226 km and the estimated survivable minimum of 80 km.

**The lesson.** A written constraint is not operational until the study names
its units and conditions and assigns a check at the interface where the value
is consumed. Architecture tool paths cross many such interfaces, and a clean
run cannot repair a missing contract.
:::

@fig-ontology-chain shows the full set of dependencies without filling them in
prematurely. Formulation supplies the question and claim. Later work must still
represent the design state, choose methods, make tool requests executable,
return results, and review what those results support.

![**A bounded study connects a scoped question to an architecture decision.** The architect establishes the scope and claim, while later work supplies represented state, tools, execution, results, review, and a named decision owner.](images/F4-ontology-chain){#fig-ontology-chain width="85%" fig-alt="A common structure connecting a scoped architecture study and its architectural claim to represented state, tools, an execution and analysis process, results, review, a named decision owner, and a scoped finding or decision."}

## Why the Work Has Distinct Stages

A stage is not a calendar milestone or a team boundary. It identifies work that
can be adequate while the adjacent work is inadequate, and whose failure sends
the study to a different repair.

The default decomposition has six stages.

1. **Formulate** declares the bounded study.
2. **Explore** produces legal candidates or determines that no candidate
   remains expressible inside the permitted space.
3. **Implement** turns a candidate into an executable tool request and records
   whether the requested work actually ran.
4. **Evaluate** compares the returned measurements with the study's checks.
5. **Explain** tests whether the proposed mechanism accounts for the result.
6. **Review and Decide** determines what the cumulative record supports and
   records the next action or stop.

Six is a useful default, not a property of all architecture work. Adjacent
stages can be combined when they answer the same question, produce the same
output, and share the same repair. They should remain separate when any of
those differ. @tbl-stage-seams applies this test to each adjacent boundary.

| **Boundary** | **Different questions and outputs** | **Different inadequacy and repair** |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Formulate → Explore | Formulate asks what decision the study may support and produces a study contract. Explore asks which candidates exist inside that contract and produces candidates plus a search record. | An inadequate contract returns to the question, scope, or constraints. An inadequate exploration returns to the represented space or the method request. |
| Explore → Implement | Explore asks which candidate should be tried. Implement asks whether the candidate can be expressed as a valid tool request and whether the requested work ran. | A missing or illegal candidate returns to the design space. A stale workspace, malformed request, license failure, or empty output returns to the environment or request. |
| Implement → Evaluate | Implement produces an execution record or an infrastructure failure. Evaluate produces a checked comparison. | A run that never executed cannot count against the candidate. A completed run whose result fails a declared check can. |
| Evaluate → Explain | Evaluate asks whether the measured result clears the planned comparison. Explain asks whether the proposed design mechanism produced that result. | A measurement problem returns to the measurement plan or candidate. A mechanism problem returns to the hypothesis, retained observations, or contrast used to test it. |
| Explain → Review and Decide | Explain produces a supported, revised, or failed mechanism account. Review and Decide asks what that account and the checked result permit the study to conclude. | An incomplete explanation returns to the hypothesis or study. A record that cannot support the intended decision narrows the conclusion, reopens a named stage, or stops honestly. |

: **Stage boundaries exist where questions, outputs, or repairs differ.** The
table states all five seams so that the six-stage default can be challenged or
folded for another project. {#tbl-stage-seams tbl-colwidths="[20,41,39]"}

Iteration rate and human involvement do not follow the stage names. An
analytical exploration may run thousands of candidates unattended, while a
new action space may require sustained architect judgment. An evaluation check
may be mechanical, while deciding whether the workload represents deployment
may not be. Tool cost, review needs, and decision scope determine how quickly a
stage can run and who must take part. @fig-ontology-loop summarizes the default
without assigning a fixed iteration rate or participant to any stage.

![**A six-stage default for one bounded architecture study.** The stages carry a study from formulation through candidates, executable work, checked results, mechanism testing, and a recorded decision or stop. The illustrated return path shows one contract repair going back to Formulate; other repairs return to the stage that owns the inadequate output.](images/ch3-ontology-loop){#fig-ontology-loop width="100%" fig-alt="Six numbered stages arranged in two rows. Formulate, Explore, Implement, Evaluate, Explain, and Review and Decide carry one bounded study forward. One illustrated contract repair returns to Formulate, while other repairs may return to the stage that owns the inadequate output."}

The Evaluate-to-Explain boundary deserves special attention because a favorable
number can survive evaluation while the proposed mechanism fails. Gupta and
colleagues used an evolutionary coding agent to write last-level cache
replacement policies for ChampSim [@GoberEtAl2022ChampSim;
@GuptaEtAl2026ArchAgent]. One generated policy appeared to improve IPC by
bypassing writes that then disappeared from the modeled memory system. The
simulator score improved, but the improvement did not come from a valid cache
mechanism. The authors identified the simulator escape by inspecting and testing
the policy.

That case does not show that every result needs an elaborate causal proof. It
shows that clearing a metric and accounting for the metric are different
questions. A study can merge Evaluate and Explain when the check itself
establishes the relevant mechanism, as a timing violation may do for an
oversized SRAM. It should keep them separate when a search can exploit the
measurement setup without realizing the intended design behavior.

## What Each Stage Must Produce

The lifecycle becomes useful only when each stage has a contract.
@tbl-stage-contracts states what each stage receives, what it must produce, what
makes the output adequate for this study, and where repair goes when it is not
adequate.

| **Stage** | **Receives** | **Produces and checks** | **Repair and handoff** |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Formulate | Diagnosed work, preserved checks, product intent, and known constraints. | A study contract whose question, comparator, scope, changes, conditions, measurements, budget, stop, decision, and exclusions agree with one another. | Repair the question or scope. Hand the contract to Explore without choosing a method for it. |
| Explore | The study contract and, once available, a represented set of legal changes. | One or more legal candidates, or a record that no candidate remains expressible or clears a declared cheap prerequisite. | Repair the representation or method request. Hand a named candidate and its selection history to Implement. |
| Implement | A candidate, requested tool work, budget, and required inputs. | An execution record showing the requested work ran on the intended state, or a typed infrastructure failure showing that it did not. | Repair the request or environment. Hand completed tool returns to Evaluate; never treat an unevaluated candidate as rejected. |
| Evaluate | Completed tool returns, comparator, planned metrics, thresholds, and validity conditions. | A comparison stating which checks passed, failed, or remain unresolved, together with the observations Explain will need. | Repair the measurement plan, rerun within budget, or reject the candidate on a declared check. Hand a checked result to Explain. |
| Explain | The checked result, proposed mechanism, and retained observations. | A mechanism account supported, revised, or contradicted by a declared contrast, ablation, or direct physical reason. | Repair the hypothesis or request missing observations. Hand the result and mechanism disposition to Review and Decide. |
| Review and Decide | The contract and cumulative record from all prior stages. | A decision within the declared scope, a narrower conclusion, a named repair, or an honest stop with unresolved questions. | Reopen the stage that owns the missing output or close the study. Hand the updated record forward. |

: **Each stage has a compact contract.** The stage descriptions name inputs,
outputs, adequacy, repair, and handoff without prescribing the representation,
method, tool interface, or review procedure that later chapters develop.
{#tbl-stage-contracts tbl-colwidths="[15,25,34,26]"}

This parallel form prevents the lifecycle from becoming six miniature
technical treatments.
@sec-data-representations-world-models decides how the live state and permitted
changes become visible. @sec-methods-generation-prediction-optimization compares
generation, prediction, optimization, and conventional methods.
@sec-architecture-environments-tool-interfaces makes tool requests executable
and recoverable. @sec-feedback-verification-trust develops measurement,
verification, and interpretation. @sec-running-the-loop fills a complete
execution-backed record, and @sec-what-architect-owns develops organizational
responsibility and commitment.

One distinction belongs here because it defines the Implement-to-Evaluate
boundary. A tool crash, stale workspace, malformed timing constraint, license
timeout, empty netlist, or clean exit that analyzed no paths is an
infrastructure result. It does not establish that the candidate is bad. A
candidate becomes rejectable only after the requested work executed on the
intended state and a declared architecture or physical check failed.
@sec-architecture-environments-tool-interfaces develops the detailed failure
and recovery taxonomy.

Higher fidelity also does not widen the contract. Moving from an analytical
model to cycle-level simulation, synthesis, or physical analysis may improve
the measurement of the same question. It does not authorize a decision that
the study excluded. The budget declares which work is affordable; the intended
decision declares what that work may support.

> **Architecture design loop.** The repeated process of examining the current
> design, making an allowed change, running relevant tools, interpreting the
> result, and deciding whether to revise, reject, continue, or stop. Established
> agile hardware practices provide one lineage for such iteration
> [@Izraelevitz2017Chisel].

## One Study Through the Lifecycle

The cache study can now pass through the six contracts without pretending that
an illustrative run is a completed product decision. @fig-design-loop shows the
relationship among represented state, permitted change, tool work, review, and
the next decision.

![**An iterative architecture study keeps the question connected to each tool run and decision.** An architect or method reads the recorded state, makes an allowed change, runs a tool, and submits the result for review. The study record retains what the result supports and what happens next.](images/F3-design-loop){#fig-design-loop width="85%" fig-alt="A design loop within a scoped architecture study. Recorded state, a permitted change, tool feedback, review, and the next decision remain connected."}

1. **Formulate.** The study adopts @tbl-bounded-study-contract. Its intended
   decision is which, if either, larger cache should advance to RTL evaluation,
   not whether the subsystem is ready to implement.

2. **Explore.** The declared space contains only 2\ MB, 3\ MB, and 4\ MB. The 2\ MB
   implementation already exists, but it must be rerun under the pinned study
   conditions. The 3\ MB and 4\ MB candidates are legal proposals. Explore has
   not established that either should advance.

3. **Implement.** The inexpensive SRAM evaluations run before the cycle-level
   executions. They report 1.2\ mm^2^ and 2.1\ ns for 2\ MB, 1.4\ mm^2^ and
   2.4\ ns for 3\ MB, and 1.7\ mm^2^ and 2.8\ ns for 4\ MB. The four
   cycle-level executions are then the pinned 2\ MB baseline, a 3\ MB attempt
   that resumes from stale constraints, and two clean 3\ MB runs, one of which
   is the declared repeatability check. The stale attempt is an infrastructure
   failure and says nothing about the candidate. Across the clean 3\ MB
   returns, capacity misses fall by 12 percent relative to baseline, cache
   leakage rises by 2\ mW, and modeled subsystem dynamic plus leakage power
   rises from 2.90\ W to 2.94\ W. Paired block resampling of matched baseline
   and candidate frame sequences estimates a 0.3\ ms reduction in
   99th-percentile frame time, with an illustrative 95% interval from
   -0.1\ ms to 0.7\ ms. The interval comes from the matched frames, not from
   treating two executions as a sufficient statistical sample.

4. **Evaluate.** The area and access-time checks reject 4\ MB before an
   expensive cycle-level execution. The 3\ MB results clear the modeled power,
   area, and access-time checks, but the interval around the tail-latency
   reduction crosses zero. Fewer capacity misses are not a substitute for a
   resolved frame-time result. The comparison marks 3\ MB unresolved rather
   than promoting it.

5. **Explain.** Retained miss classifications support the proposed mechanism
   that 3\ MB removes capacity misses. They do not establish that the reduction
   improves tail frame time. The mechanism is supported within the recorded
   simulator behavior, while the intended outcome remains uncertain.

6. **Review and Decide.** The baseline run, failed infrastructure run, and two
   clean 3\ MB runs consume the four-run budget. The study rejects 4\ MB on its
   cheap physical checks, leaves 3\ MB unresolved, and stops because the
   declared cycle-level budget is spent. It recommends a new study with enough
   tail observations to resolve the decision interval. It does not recommend
   either larger cache for RTL evaluation and does not weaken the later thermal
   or IR-drop review.

The sequence separates three outcomes that the earlier version blended
together. The stale-state run says nothing about the candidate. The 4\ MB area
and access-time failures reject one candidate. The budget stop closes this study
without resolving 3\ MB. A later study may reopen the question with a new
budget and additional observations, but it does not rewrite this stop as a
pass. A successful completion would be different again. It would end because
the declared decision had been resolved with every required check present, not
because a candidate failed or the budget ran out.

::: {.callout-lighthouse title="A 3\ W claim needs a complete comparison"}
**Context.** A power result becomes useful only when a reviewer can see which
workload, candidate, tool state, software assumptions, and power components it
describes.

**In this study.** The 3\ MB candidate's modeled 2.94\ W result remains inside
the 3\ W envelope, but the intended decision also depends on a resolved
tail-latency comparison and later independent physical review. Passing one
check does not resolve another or replace the preserved thermal and IR-drop
verdicts.
:::

The same stage boundary catches a more extreme infrastructure failure.

::: {.callout-failure-mode title="The tool reported a chip that did not exist"}
**The trap.** An automated search reports 0.0\ W and 0.0\ mm^2^ with a successful
tool exit.

**What happened.** The request selected no valid top-level design and also
omitted the primary clock. Elaboration contained none of the expected
instances, timing analysis had no constrained paths, and a downstream parser
substituted zeros for absent power and area fields.

**The disposition.** This is an infrastructure failure, not a breakthrough and
not a rejected candidate. A useful Implement check confirms that the expected
clocks, instances, paths, and outputs exist before Evaluate interprets their
numbers.

This is a composite of a recurring tool-flow failure pattern rather than one
published incident.
:::

## A Study Record Another Architect Can Review {#sec-design-loop-card}

A bounded study needs one cumulative record. The record starts with the study
contract and adds the output, status, and repair from each stage. It is not a
certificate of quality. Its first job is to keep missing work, failed
alternatives, remaining uncertainty, the stopping reason, and the supported
decision findable.

> **Study record.** The cumulative account of one bounded architecture study.
> It retains the contract, stage outputs, failed or unevaluated work, unresolved
> questions, stopping reason, and supported decision, with links to the detailed
> artifacts needed for review or replay.

The existing design-loop card is a compact index into that record.

> **Design-loop card.** A short guide to one architecture study. It points to
> the question, scope, stage outputs, evidence, stop, and decision. Detailed
> design state, tool returns, and replay artifacts remain in linked records.

Model cards provide a useful precedent for concise disclosure
[@MitchellEtAl2019ModelCards], but an architecture study also has changes,
tools, physical checks, rejected candidates, and a decision boundary. The
twelve existing card fields remain stable for backward compatibility with the
public templates, schemas, examples, and validators that use them. Together
they cover the study intent, executable setup, work and failures, checks,
supported finding, and recorded decision. They remain an index rather than
a claim that twelve is the only possible field count. The Explain output is
linked from Evidence and summarized under What the evidence supports.
@tbl-design-loop-card-fields shows how the fields index the illustrative cache
study without pretending that every later chapter has already supplied its
answer.

| **Field** | **The cache study's current entry** |
| --- | --- |
| Intent | Improve XR subsystem efficiency without weakening the declared physical checks. |
| Task | Decide which, if either, of the 3\ MB and 4\ MB L2 candidates should advance to RTL evaluation. |
| Design space | The 2\ MB baseline and 3\ MB and 4\ MB candidates, with all other architectural choices fixed. |
| Representation | Required state is named, but its durable form and relationships remain open for @sec-data-representations-world-models. |
| Environment | The required simulator, power, and SRAM model work is named. Exact interfaces, isolation, and recovery remain open for @sec-architecture-environments-tool-interfaces. |
| Method role | No learned method is selected. The illustrative walkthrough enumerates the two permitted alternatives directly. |
| Feedback budget | Four cycle-level executions including infrastructure reruns, plus one SRAM timing, area, and power evaluation per candidate. The stop records that this budget was spent. |
| Evidence | Illustrative cache-miss, power, area, access-time, and tail-latency results, including the interval around the frame-time reduction and links to the retained miss classifications used to test the mechanism. |
| Failed runs and rejected alternatives | One stale-state execution is marked unevaluated. The 4\ MB candidate is rejected on the declared area and access-time checks. |
| Rejection checks and authority | Power, area, access time, and tail-latency decision checks are declared. The study owner may reject a candidate on those checks but may not waive the later thermal or IR-drop review. |
| What the evidence supports | The 4\ MB rejection, a supported capacity-miss mechanism for 3\ MB, and no recommendation to advance 3\ MB because its frame-time improvement remains unresolved. |
| Decision | The architect records a budget stop and the need for a study with enough tail observations to resolve the interval. Product commitment and detailed organizational authority remain outside this chapter. |

: **The card indexes the cumulative study record rather than replacing it.**
An undeclared or unfinished entry remains visible, and the stopping reason stays
attached to the decision the record can support. {#tbl-design-loop-card-fields tbl-colwidths="[24,76]"}

The public [YAML template](https://arch2.mlsysbook.ai/design-loop-card/template.yaml),
[Markdown template](https://arch2.mlsysbook.ai/design-loop-card/template.md),
and [JSON schema](https://arch2.mlsysbook.ai/schemas/design-loop-card.v2.schema.json)
provide machine-readable forms. Validation can check the shape and links of a
card. It cannot decide that the underlying study was adequate. The complete
execution-backed example in @sec-running-the-loop shows how the open entries
become concrete records. @fig-design-loop-card-example shows the compact index
that remains at this stage. It uses a broader Lighthouse accelerator comparison
rather than the cache example above to show that the same fields can index
different studies.

![**A design-loop card is a compact index into one architecture study.** This separate Lighthouse accelerator example helps a reviewer find the study scope, stage outputs, checks, missing work, stop, and decision without treating the card as proof.](images/F4b-design-loop-card-example){#fig-design-loop-card-example width="85%" fig-alt="A compact study index card for a Lighthouse accelerator comparison, pointing from the question and scope to the work, checks, stopping reason, and recorded decision."}

The record also makes the handoff to
@sec-data-representations-world-models precise. The study has named the state it
needs, including cache parameters, workload and software versions, constraints,
histories, and permitted changes. It has not yet represented their
relationships, freshness, invariants, or unknowns in a form a method can inspect
and change safely.

## Open Research Questions

The six-stage default and cumulative record remain proposals to test rather
than rules to assume.

**What is the smallest study contract that still prevents a tool or reviewer
from changing the question without noticing?** The answer may vary by decision,
but removing a declaration should produce a failure that can be observed rather
than only a preference for more documentation.

**When can two adjacent stages be combined without hiding the source of a
failure?** Independent projects could test whether the question, output, and
repair criteria predict which boundaries remain useful in practice.

**How should a study route repair when more than one stage is inadequate?** A
stale workload, weak representation, failed tool request, and unresolved metric
can coexist, so repair needs an order that does not mistake the most visible
failure for the first one to fix.

**Which stopping conditions distinguish an honest unresolved result from a
premature end to exploration?** Candidate rejection, budget exhaustion,
exhausted alternatives, missing information, and a completed decision are
different stops and should leave different records.

**Should infrastructure failures consume the same budget as completed
evaluations?** They consume licenses, compute, schedule, and engineering time
even when they say nothing about the candidate, which makes both answers
defensible for different budgets.

**How much of a high-volume study record must remain replayable?** Preserving
every intermediate artifact may cost more than it saves, while preserving only
the final candidate can make the stopping reason and failed alternatives
impossible to audit.

**Does mechanically checkable record completeness improve independent replay
or expose a changed study question?** Comparative studies could measure whether
required fields and resolvable links help a new team reproduce the stop or
detect that a comparator, exclusion, or intended decision changed.

**Under what conditions does the six-stage default fail to improve a study?**
A useful lifecycle should be removable or foldable when it adds record-keeping
cost without producing clearer outputs, repairs, decisions, or stops.

## Conclusion

::: {.callout-design-principle title="Bound the study before choosing the method"}
A method cannot repair an unstated question, comparator, budget, or stopping
condition. Declare the intended decision and the work that could support it
before deciding where AI belongs.
:::

@sec-design-loop-no-longer-scales supplied a diagnosed piece of review work and
a check that an intervention must preserve. The cache comparison here was the
technical content of one review package, not a claim that cache search caused
or solved the queue. This chapter turned that content into two concrete outputs.
The study contract declares what one bounded comparison may change, measure,
spend, decide, and exclude. The cumulative record keeps the contract connected
to stage outputs, failed or unevaluated work, unresolved questions, the
stopping reason, and the decision actually supported.

The six stages are a default decomposition for producing that record. Their
names matter less than the boundary test. Keep adjacent work separate when it
answers a different question, produces a different output, or needs a different
repair. Fold it when those distinctions do not exist. Human involvement and
iteration speed follow the work and checks, not a permanent division between
human and machine stages.

The Lighthouse walkthrough showed why the distinctions matter. A stale-state
run was an infrastructure failure, the 4\ MB area and access-time results
rejected one candidate, and the exhausted cycle-level budget stopped the study
without resolving the 3\ MB tail-latency comparison. None of those outcomes
authorizes the same next action. Recording them separately lets a later
architect repair the right part of the work instead of reading every
unsuccessful turn as a bad design.

The study is now declared but not yet live. Its hardware and software state,
relationships, permitted changes, histories, freshness, and unknowns still need
a representation that preserves their architectural and physical meaning.
That is the work of @sec-data-representations-world-models.
